match.reason: The closest bank point covers implicit values through word choice and assumptions, but it does not teach the brief's ideas of what a text leaves out or whose perspective it centres, so a new point is needed.

draft.title: Implicit values
card: A value is something a text treats as important or right. An explicit value is stated outright. An implicit value is carried without being stated, and the reader works it out.
Normal
what the text treats as ordinary or expected. If every family in an advertisement lives in a large house, it quietly suggests that this is how people live.
Centred
who gets the focus, the voice and the sympathy. Whose view the reader sees through shapes whose view seems to matter.
Left out
who or what is missing. Silence can suggest that a group or view is unimportant, though it can also have other causes.
draft.remember: Ask what a text treats as normal, who it centres and what it leaves out.

a.q: A news story about a flood quotes only the mayor and a business owner. Residents who lost homes are not quoted. Which implicit value does this most suggest?
opts: Officials and owners matter more than residents
Floods are less serious than people think
Residents should speak only in private
The reporter dislikes the mayor
a.why: The story centres two voices and leaves out the residents, which suggests their views count for less. The text never states this, so it is implicit. Nothing in the story suggests the reporter's feelings about the mayor.
a.clue: Look at whose voices are included and whose are missing.

b.q: A novel's narrator describes a character's rowing club as having a plain, ordinary membership. All the members are wealthy, and the narrator never mentions money. What implicit value does this show?
opts: Wealth is treated as normal and not worth remarking on
Rowing is a sport only for the wealthy
Money is openly condemned by the narrator
The narrator wants the reader to join the club
b.why: The narrator calls the club ordinary while its members are all wealthy, so wealth is treated as the normal state. The narrator never mentions money, so nothing is stated outright. The text does not condemn money, because it does not mention it at all.
b.clue: What does the narrator treat as ordinary without comment?

a.best: Officials and owners matter more than residents

b.best: Wealth is treated as normal and not worth remarking on

problems.detail: The right option is the longest. Its wording ('treated as normal and not worth remarking on') closely restates the clue ('treat as ordinary without comment') and the card's key word 'normal', so a student could match words rather than infer the value.

b.q: In a novel, every friend of the main family owns a holiday house and sends their children to private schools. The narrator presents their lives as ordinary and never mentions money. What implicit value does this suggest?
opts: A wealthy lifestyle is how most people live
Private schools give students a better education
The narrator openly criticises the rich family
Readers should save up to buy a holiday house
b.why: Every family has the same wealth and the narrator never comments on it, so the text quietly suggests this is how people live. The novel says nothing about the quality of private schools, and an open criticism would be explicit, not implicit. Here there is no criticism at all.
b.clue: What does the narrator's silence about money suggest?

a.best: Officials and owners matter more than residents

b.best: A wealthy lifestyle is how most people live
